match.reason: None of the bank points teaches legal capacity (the age at which the law grants rights and duties such as working, driving and voting), so the new point needs its own card.

note:
A fresh check found these problems in this version. Fix each one, and keep everything that is right:
- Question a, other: The clue 'Think about what the law assumes about older people' echoes the right option ('It assumes older people can take more responsibility') almost word for word, so a student can match it without knowing the idea.
- Question a, wording: The question asks why rights have different ages, but the intended answer explains why the law uses age at all. The card does not say why voting and driving have different ages, so the question and answer do not quite match.

rejected.title: Legal capacity and age
card: Legal capacity is a person's ability to hold legal rights and duties. It lets a person do things the law recognises, such as make a binding contract or be responsible for their actions.
The law grants many rights and duties by age. A person gains them as they grow older, because the law assumes older people are better able to make decisions and take responsibility.

In New South Wales, a person must be 16 to get a learner licence and 18 to vote in elections. The law also limits the work children can do, such as through safety rules and limits on some kinds of jobs.
Each right has its own age, so a person can have some rights before others. Having one right, such as a learner licence, does not give a person another, such as the vote.
rejected.remember: The law grants legal rights and duties as people reach set ages.

a.q: Why does the law set different ages for rights such as voting and driving?
opts: It assumes older people can take more responsibility
It says people under 18 have no legal rights
It gives all rights at birth and removes them later
It lets each person pick the age they gain a right
a.why: The law uses age as a guide to when people can handle the duties that come with a right. It does not take away all rights from young people, so the option saying under 18s have no legal rights is wrong.
a.clue: Think about what the law assumes about older people.

b.q: Jaya is 17 and lives in Wagga Wagga. She wants to vote in the next state election. What is the legal position?
opts: She cannot vote yet, because the voting age is 18
She can vote, because she can already hold a learner licence
She can vote, because she already has a part-time job
She can vote if her parents give written permission
b.why: Voting is a right the law grants at 18, so Jaya has to wait. Being able to hold a learner licence or having a job does not give her the right to vote, because each right has its own age.
b.clue: Each right has its own age set by law.
